name: EDMONDSON, J.
description: Concurred, delivered the opinion of the Court, arguing that the EDEA creates an unconstitutional 'dual purpose' for OPERS's investment decisions, conflicting with the Oklahoma Constitution's mandate for an 'exclusive purpose' for public retirement funds.

name: Kuehn, V.C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that HB 2783 unconstitutionally changes the fixed seven-year terms of TSET directors to at-will terms, subverting the constitutional intent to protect TSET funds from legislative or executive diversion.

name: GURICH, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Senate Bill 632 is unconstitutional because it creates business court divisions whose judges are district judges but are appointed rather than elected, violating Article VII, Section 9 of the Oklahoma Constitution.

name: ROWE, C.J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that the Legislature can create a new division within an enumerated court, but S.B. 632's provisions for selecting judges conflict with constitutional requirements for judicial election, making it unconstitutional.

name: KUEHN, V.C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Court should not exercise original jurisdiction because Petitioners failed to establish standing and there was no public urgency, and the case lacked a proper factual record.

name: JETT, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Court should not assume original jurisdiction as there was no pressing need for an expedited decision, especially since interim injunctive relief could prevent alleged harm.

name: KANE, J.
description: Did not vote on the case.

name: KANE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that current residency restrictions for sex offenders are not punitive and can be applied retroactively without violating ex post facto clauses.

name: KUEHN, V.C.J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, arguing that the prior Starkey precedent should be overturned and SORA deemed a civil statute, but that the record was insufficient to determine if the residency restrictions were punitive in effect.

name: COMBS, J.
description: Dissented, arguing that applying the current residency restrictions retroactively increases punishment for Donaldson, violating the ex post facto clause of the Oklahoma Constitution.

name: Combs, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that there is no irreconcilable conflict between the GTCA and the OADA regarding notice provisions, and therefore GTCA notice is required for discrimination claims against governmental entities.

name: DARBY, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Governor has statutory and constitutional authority to represent the state's interests and choose counsel, and the Attorney General cannot assume control over the Governor's objection.

name: Combs
description: Concurred, argued that the Governor's participation includes the choice of counsel and the Attorney General can appear ex officio, but believes the underlying case is moot due to previous rulings invalidating the compacts.

name: LUMPKIN, Judge
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court abused its discretion by applying the Exclusionary Rule to suppress evidence for a 'knock and announce' rule violation, as the rule's purpose is not to shield evidence and other deterrents exist.

name: ROWLAND, P.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the exclusionary rule should rarely be employed for statutory violations unless the statute explicitly provides for it, and overruled prior inconsistent case law.

name: MUSSEMAN, V.P.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the exclusionary rule is inapplicable and highlighted concerns about the court's standard of review and district courts exceeding the scope of motions to quash.

name: EDMONDSON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that local school boards possess statutory authority to maintain and control their local school libraries, including discretionary selection of books based on local community standards, and the State Board of Education lacks authority to overrule this discretion.

name: KAUGER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the medical district is subject to lawsuits through its board of trustees to the same extent as municipalities and counties, and the GTCA applies to preclude recovery when workers' compensation benefits have been awarded.

name: Rowe, V.C.J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that public charter schools must be nonsectarian under the Oklahoma Constitution but dissented from the remainder of the majority's opinion.

name: Kuehn, J.
description: Dissented, argued that St. Isidore would not become a "state actor" merely by contracting with the State for educational choice, and that excluding private entities based on religious affiliation would violate the Free Exercise Clause.

name: KUEHN
description: Concurred in part, dissented in part, argued that Initiative Petition 446 should go to a vote but the court should not determine its constitutionality pre-election.

name: KANE, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the proposed initiative petition violates the non-delegation doctrine, is not severable, and has a faulty gist.

name: ROWE, V.C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the court should follow precedent and strike the initiative petition for constitutional infirmities (like non-delegation doctrine and misleading gist) before it goes to a vote.

name: MUSSEMAN, JUDGE
description: Concurred, argued that Oklahoma district courts' subject matter jurisdiction is not preempted by federal law in Indian Country, and the petitioner waived his jurisdictional claim by not raising it earlier.

name: ROWLAND, PRESIDING JUDGE
description: Concurred, argued that criminal jurisdiction in Indian Country does not implicate the State of Oklahoma's subject matter jurisdiction, which is established by the Oklahoma Constitution and cannot be taken away by Congress, and that Deo waived his McGirt claim.

name: LUMPKIN, JUDGE
description: Concurred, argued that the opinion correctly defines subject matter jurisdiction and clarifies how it may be preempted, emphasizing that Oklahoma district courts have broad jurisdiction and Indian tribes have limited sovereignty as "domestic dependent nations."

name: HUDSON, VICE PRESIDING JUDGE
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's approach conflicts with established federal law, particularly Castro-Huerta, by mischaracterizing Indian Country jurisdictional challenges and ignoring the Bracker balancing test, and that the petitioner did not waive his claim.

name: LEWIS, JUDGE
description: Dissented, argued that states have no jurisdiction over crimes committed by Indians in Indian Country unless expressly conferred by Congress, and that Castro-Huerta does not apply to Indian defendants in Indian Country, and that the petitioner's claim was not waived.

name: ROWE, V.C.J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the Legislature had the constitutional authority to consider the bills during a concurrent special session, the legislation did not exceed the call of the special session, and the Governor's authority to negotiate State-Tribal compacts is statutory, not constitutional, and was not infringed upon.

name: KUEHN, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, arguing that while the Legislature can repeal delegated authority, it cannot micro-manage the Governor's execution of that authority, and the bills constitute impermissible legislative meddling that violates the separation-of-powers doctrine.

name: COMBS, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the three Acts placed unnecessary burdens on the lawful termination of a pregnancy and the trial court erred in denying a temporary injunction.

name: Kauger
description: Concurred, argued that any analysis of an abortion statute must consider the life of the mother.

name: Kane, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the outright ban on abortions remains law and the majority's analysis fails to consider the rights of the unborn.

name: Rowe, V.C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Court had already upheld the constitutionality of a statute prohibiting elective abortion, making the majority's current stance inconsistent and misleading.

name: Darby, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the district court did not abuse its discretion by applying existing precedent and the majority misapplied the standard of review.

name: Kuehn, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Oklahoma Constitution does not support a right to abortion and the majority's decision is based on speculation rather than evidence considered under current law.

name: EDMONDSON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the petition failed to state a claim that the Lengthy Trial Fund fee statute is an unconstitutional special law, finding the legislative determination regarding litigant classification to be reasonable.

name: DARBY
description: Concurred, argued that while he would dissent if the issue were new, stare decisis dictates the outcome based on previous rulings.

name: KANE, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the case presents different legal and factual issues than the previous case (OCRJ I) and stare decisis alone does not fully resolve it, and applying stare decisis could expand the reach of OCRJ I, which he believes was wrongly decided.

name: ROWE, V.C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that S.B. 1503 is distinguishable from the statute found unconstitutional in OCRJ I because S.B. 1503 places discretion with the physician to determine a medical emergency, which would have alleviated concerns in the prior case, and that the majority's characterization of S.B. 1503 as "even more extreme" is misplaced.

name: KUEHN, J.
description: Dissented, argued for the reasons given in his dissent in Oklahoma Call for Reproductive Justice v. Drummond.

name: GURICH, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Commission's interpretation of Section 69 is consistent with legislative intent and avoids constitutional issues by giving the claimant the benefit of the longer limitations period, making the phrase "whichever is greater" superfluous, and upholding due process by preventing employers from shortening the statute of limitations without notice.

name: KANE, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority disregarded the clear and unambiguous statutory language by re-inserting "whichever is greater" after the Legislature explicitly deleted it in 2019, thereby substituting its own wisdom for legislative intent, and believes the statute clearly states a six-month limitation if benefits were paid.

name: KUEHN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority disregarded the clear and unambiguous statutory language by re-inserting "whichever is greater" after the Legislature explicitly deleted it in 2019, thereby substituting its own wisdom for legislative intent, and believes the statute clearly states a six-month limitation if benefits were paid.

name: DOWNING, S.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority disregarded the clear and unambiguous statutory language by re-inserting "whichever is greater" after the Legislature explicitly deleted it in 2019, thereby substituting its own wisdom for legislative intent, and believes the statute clearly states a six-month limitation if benefits were paid.

name: KAUGER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the right to preserve the life of the mother is deeply rooted in Oklahoma law and highlighted the incongruity of the challenged statute.

name: COMBS, J.
description: Concurred specially, argued that Article II, Section 2 of the Oklahoma Constitution provides a substantive right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, including personal autonomy and a right to privacy, which confers greater rights than the U.S. Constitution.

name: KANE, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority fashioned a right that does not exist in the Oklahoma Constitution, confusing what is provided with what is wished, and that the issue should be decided by the people.

name: ROWE, V.C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that abortion policy is a political question for the people to decide, not the court, and that the Oklahoma Constitution does not protect a right to abortion.

name: DARBY, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority created a new constitutional right based on a statutory exception, applied an incorrect standard of review, and was perplexed by the court's claim of not ruling on elective abortion while doing so.

name: KUEHN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the court should exercise judicial restraint and not create a right where none explicitly exists in the Oklahoma Constitution, leaving policy decisions to the Legislature and the people.

name: KANE, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that Oklahoma law does not recognize a cause of action for a voluntarily intoxicated adult against a commercial vendor for self-inflicted injuries or against a bettor for injuries sustained while driving intoxicated.

name: ROWE, V.C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that while the facts are appalling, the court should not expand civil liability beyond common law or statutory mandates, as this responsibility rests with the Legislature.

name: Kauger, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's conclusion that the mother of the driver has no cause of action is contrary to the Oklahoma Constitution and statutes, which impose a broad duty to refrain from selling alcohol to intoxicated persons.

name: Gurich, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the court's precedent in Ohio Casualty has no basis in law because the State Constitution and statutes impose a broad duty to refrain from selling alcohol to an intoxicated person, and the concept of 'voluntary consumption' should not negate the cause of action.

name: Darby, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the egregious facts of the case, where employees over-served and then bet an intoxicated person to drive, should allow for a cause of action, and the court's public policy reasoning for protecting innocent third parties but not the intoxicated driver is flawed.

name: Combs, J.
description: Other, was disqualified from the case.

name: KAUGER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that PTCs are intangible personal property and are exempt from ad valorem taxation under the Oklahoma Constitution, affirming the trial court's exclusion of PTCs from valuation.

name: KAUGER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the statutes were an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority to the extent they required the Governor to declare an emergency for local school districts to make health decisions.

name: FISCHER, S.J.
description: Concurred in part with the majority regarding the unconstitutional delegation of legislative power in section 1210.190, but dissented from upholding section 1210.189, arguing it is an unconstitutional special law regulating public schools.

name: COMBS, J.
description: Concurred in part with the majority regarding the unconstitutional delegation of legislative power in section 1210.190, but dissented from upholding section 1210.189, arguing it is an unconstitutional special law regulating public schools.

name: ROWE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that admitting prejudicial evidence and jury instructions violated parents' right to a fair trial.

name: DARBY, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court's admission of prejudicial evidence deprived parents of constitutional due process and a fair trial.

name: COMBS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that any error was harmless given overwhelming evidence of abuse and that the majority applied the wrong standard of harmless error review.
